plan: Both blind solvers rated batch 1 too easy because its distractors were plainly unsupported. This batch is a paired-passage set (ACT Reading includes one) with partly-true distractors: 3 items on Passage A, 3 on Passage B, and 3 on both, as Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. Both authors are invented and the passages argue opinions, keeping factual claims general. Also re-submits R001-09 relabelled easy (text unchanged).

passages.title: SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by an urban ecologist; Passage B is from an essay by a city planner. Both are original texts written for this practice set.
passages.text:
Passage A

For much of the last century, cities treated small streams as problems to be solved. A creek that flooded a neighborhood or carried away sewage was straightened, lined with concrete, and eventually sealed inside a pipe beneath the street. Out of sight, the stream stopped being anyone's concern.

In recent decades, a number of cities have begun to reverse that choice by "daylighting" buried streams: removing the pavement above them and rebuilding a channel open to the sky. Supporters often lead with the ecological case. An open channel, lined with gravel and shaded by plants, can support insects, fish, and birds that a dark pipe cannot. Exposed water also cools the air around it on hot days.

But the most persuasive argument may be the practical one. A pipe has a fixed capacity; when a storm sends more water than it can carry, the excess backs up into basements and streets. A restored stream with a wide, shallow floodplain can spread that water out and slow it down. In this sense, daylighting does not merely decorate a city; it gives the city room to absorb storms that pipes were never built for.

Daylighting is not cheap, and it is not always possible. Where buildings now sit directly above an old stream, the cost of restoration can be prohibitive. Yet the cities that have tried it often report a benefit no engineer predicted: people come. They walk along the water at lunch, bring children to look for minnows, and begin to treat the neighborhood as a place worth caring for. A stream that was once a problem to be hidden becomes, in a sense, a public room.

Passage B

Proposals to daylight buried streams are easy to love. Few people object to the image of clear water running where there was once only asphalt. As a city planner, though, I have learned to ask what such projects cost and what else the same money might do.

The answer is often sobering. Opening a stream through a dense neighborhood can mean acquiring property, rerouting utility lines, and rebuilding streets, work that may cost many times as much as repairing the existing pipe. For the same budget, a city might install rain gardens and permeable pavement across dozens of blocks, capturing storm water closer to where it falls.

Nor is a restored stream automatically a healthy one. Water that runs off city streets carries oil, salt, and litter. Unless the surrounding area is also changed, a daylighted stream may simply put polluted water on display. Some restored channels require years of maintenance before they support the wildlife their designers promised.

None of this means daylighting is never worth doing. Where a buried stream runs beneath an open lot or a park, the costs can be modest and the benefits real. My concern is with treating daylighting as a symbol rather than a tool. A city's first question should not be "How do we bring the stream back?" but "What is the most effective way to manage this water?" Sometimes the answer will be a stream. Often it will not.

passages.title: LITERARY NARRATIVE: "What Ready Looks Like" (an original story written for this practice set)
passages.text:
The bakery on Linden Street opened at six, but the work began at midnight. That was the first thing Mrs. Dalca told me when she hired me, the summer I was seventeen, and she said it the way other people mention the weather: a fact to be dressed for, not complained about. I nodded as if midnight were nothing. I had stayed up later than that for worse reasons.

The first week, I was useless in a way I had not known was possible. I measured flour too quickly and scattered it across the counter. I kneaded the dough as if it had insulted me. When the loaves came out of the oven flat and pale, Mrs. Dalca did not scold me. She broke one open, pressed the crumb between her fingers, and handed me half. "Taste what hurry tastes like," she said.

It tasted like nothing. That was the problem.

I wanted to be good at things immediately. At school I had been the kind of student who finished tests first and then waited, tapping a pencil, for everyone else. Speed had always looked like intelligence to me, and slowness like a kind of failure. The bakery did not care what I thought. Dough rose on its own schedule, and no amount of glaring at the proofing baskets made it rise faster.

Mrs. Dalca worked without a clock. She would lift the cloth from a bowl, press a floured finger into the dough, and watch the dent. If it sprang back at once, she covered the bowl again. If it filled in slowly, halfway, she nodded and reached for the scale. I asked her once how she knew how long to wait. She shrugged. "I don't know how long," she said. "I know what ready looks like."

By July I had stopped looking at the wall clock above the ovens. I began to notice other things instead: the sour, almost fruity smell that meant the starter was strong; the way a well-shaped loaf held its seam on the counter; the faint crackle, like distant rain, that came from the crusts as they cooled. None of these were things I could have learned faster by trying harder. They arrived when they arrived, the way the dough did.

On my last night, Mrs. Dalca let me make the rye on my own. I mixed and folded and waited, and when the loaves came out I broke one open the way she had that first week. The crumb was dark and open and smelled of caraway. I handed her half. She chewed for a long time, longer than seemed necessary, and I felt the old impatience rise in my chest. Then she nodded once, the same small nod she gave the dough.

"Now," she said, "it tastes like time."

candidates.stem: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.A: compare the construction costs of pipes and restored streams in detail.
choices.B: explain the engineering steps a city must take to restore a buried stream.
choices.C: argue that daylighting buried streams can bring ecological, practical, and social benefits despite its costs.
choices.D: criticize earlier generations of city officials for burying streams.

candidates.evidence: Daylighting is not cheap, and it is not always possible.
candidates.explanation: Passage A presents ecological benefits (wildlife, cooling), a practical benefit (flood capacity), and a social benefit (people come), while acknowledging costs. Its purpose is to make the case for daylighting.

A.rationale: Passage A mentions that daylighting is not cheap but gives no detailed cost comparison; that kind of comparison appears in Passage B.

B.rationale: The passage defines daylighting in one sentence but does not lay out engineering steps.

D.rationale: The first paragraph describes past practice neutrally ("treated small streams as problems to be solved"); it does not criticize anyone.

hints: Which choice accounts for every paragraph of Passage A?
Does the author mainly explain, compare, criticize or argue?

strategy.explanation: Summarize Passage A as 'daylighting is worth it for several reasons,' then match.

candidates.remember: Purpose covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.

candidates.stem: In Passage A, the statement that daylighting "does not merely decorate a city" primarily serves to:

choices.A: stress that daylighting provides practical flood protection in addition to its visual appeal.
choices.B: concede that daylighting's main value is how it improves a city's appearance.
choices.C: dismiss the ecological argument for daylighting as less important than appearance.
choices.D: suggest that most cities daylight streams for decorative reasons.

candidates.evidence: In this sense, daylighting does not merely decorate a city; it gives the city room to absorb storms that pipes were never built for.
candidates.explanation: The phrase comes at the end of the paragraph explaining that a restored stream can absorb storm water a pipe cannot hold. "Not merely decorate" grants that daylighting looks good but insists its real value is practical.

B.rationale: "Not merely" signals that appearance is NOT its main value, the opposite of this choice.

C.rationale: The phrase contrasts decoration with flood control, not with ecology, and the author values ecology too.

D.rationale: The passage makes no claim about most cities' motives.

hints: What does "not merely" imply about decoration?
What does the rest of the sentence emphasize?

strategy.explanation: Read the full sentence and the paragraph around it to see what is being contrasted.

candidates.remember: "Not merely X" grants X but stresses something more.

candidates.stem: The author of Passage A suggests that the increased public use of areas around restored streams was:

choices.A: the main reason most cities decided to daylight their streams.
choices.B: limited to neighborhoods where no buildings stood above the old stream.
choices.C: a direct result of reduced flooding in those neighborhoods.
choices.D: an outcome that the projects' designers had not anticipated.

candidates.evidence: Yet the cities that have tried it often report a benefit no engineer predicted: people come.
candidates.explanation: The author calls the public's response "a benefit no engineer predicted," so it was unanticipated.

A.rationale: If no one predicted the benefit, it could not have been the main reason for the projects.

B.rationale: Buildings above streams are mentioned as a cost problem, not as a limit on public use.

C.rationale: The passage describes both flood control and public use but never links one as the cause of the other.

hints: Find the sentence that introduces the people who come to the streams.
What word describes whether anyone expected it?

strategy.explanation: The phrase "no engineer predicted" answers the question directly.

candidates.remember: Stay with what the text states; don't invent causes.

candidates.stem: In Passage B, the author's central concern about daylighting is that it:

choices.A: always costs more than repairing the existing pipes.
choices.B: may be chosen for its appeal rather than for how well it manages water.
choices.C: inevitably harms the wildlife it is meant to support.
choices.D: is unpopular with the residents of the neighborhoods involved.

candidates.evidence: My concern is with treating daylighting as a symbol rather than a tool.
candidates.explanation: The author states the concern directly: daylighting should not be treated "as a symbol rather than a tool." A city should first ask how best to manage the water, and sometimes the answer is not a stream.

A.rationale: The author says daylighting "may cost many times as much" and that costs can be "modest" near open lots; "always" overstates the claim.

C.rationale: The author says some channels need years of maintenance before supporting wildlife, not that daylighting inevitably harms it.

D.rationale: The author says the proposals are "easy to love"; unpopularity is not the concern.

hints: Look for the sentence in which the author names a concern directly.
Watch for choices with words like always or inevitably.

strategy.explanation: The last paragraph states the concern; eliminate the extreme choices.

candidates.remember: Beware words like always and never.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word "sobering" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: The "answer" refers to what daylighting projects cost and what else the money could do. Calling it "sobering" means it prompts serious, careful thought, which the following details about high costs explain.

B.rationale: This is the literal, everyday meaning of "sobering," which does not fit a discussion of project costs.

C.rationale: The costs described are a reason for caution, not a pleasant surprise.

D.rationale: "Frightening" is too strong; the author is cautious, not alarmed.

hints: What "answer" is being described?
What attitude do the following sentences show?

strategy.explanation: Predict 'makes you think seriously,' then match.

candidates.remember: Context beats the most common meaning.

candidates.stem: According to Passage B, which of the following could limit the ecological benefits of a daylighted stream?

choices.A: The width of the restored channel
choices.B: The number of people who visit the stream
choices.C: Polluted runoff from the surrounding streets
choices.D: The installation of rain gardens on nearby blocks

candidates.evidence: Water that runs off city streets carries oil, salt, and litter. Unless the surrounding area is also changed, a daylighted stream may simply put polluted water on display.
candidates.explanation: Passage B warns that runoff carrying oil, salt and litter can leave a restored stream polluted unless the surrounding area also changes.

A.rationale: Passage B does not discuss channel width; Passage A mentions a wide floodplain as a benefit.

B.rationale: Visitors are discussed in Passage A as a benefit, not in Passage B as a limit.

D.rationale: Passage B presents rain gardens as an alternative way to manage water, not as a threat to a stream.

hints: Find the paragraph in Passage B about whether a restored stream is healthy.
What does the water carry?

strategy.explanation: Paragraph 3 of Passage B answers this directly.

candidates.remember: Answer from the passage the question names.

candidates.subskill: Points of agreement across paired passages
candidates.stem: The authors of both passages would most likely agree that:

choices.A: daylighting is the most effective way for a city to manage storm water.
choices.B: restored streams begin supporting wildlife as soon as they are opened.
choices.C: cities should stop repairing existing storm-water pipes.
choices.D: daylighting can be worthwhile in some places but can be very costly where buildings or streets sit above a stream.

candidates.evidence: Where a buried stream runs beneath an open lot or a park, the costs can be modest and the benefits real.
candidates.explanation: Passage A says daylighting "is not cheap" and can be "prohibitive" where buildings sit above a stream, while arguing that it brings real benefits. Passage B says costs can be many times higher in dense neighborhoods but "modest" near open lots, where the benefits are "real." Both accept that it can be worthwhile in some places and very costly in others.

A.rationale: Passage B explicitly doubts this, suggesting rain gardens and permeable pavement may be more effective in many cases.

B.rationale: Passage B says some channels need years of maintenance before supporting wildlife.

C.rationale: Neither author argues for abandoning pipe repair; Passage B treats repair as a cheaper option.

hints: Find what each passage says about cost.
Does either passage say daylighting can be worthwhile in some cases?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate any choice that one author would reject; the survivor must fit both.

candidates.remember: Agreement questions: the answer must fit both authors.

author_checklist.hardness: must reconcile both passages; three choices fit one author at most

candidates.subskill: Predicting one author's response to the other
candidates.stem: Based on Passage B, how would its author most likely respond to Passage A's claim that a restored stream "can spread that water out and slow it down"?

choices.A: By denying that a restored stream can slow down storm water at all
choices.B: By noting that other methods, such as rain gardens and permeable pavement, might manage storm water more cost-effectively across a wider area
choices.C: By agreeing that daylighting should be a city's first choice for managing storm water
choices.D: By arguing that flooding is rarely a serious problem in cities

candidates.evidence: For the same budget, a city might install rain gardens and permeable pavement across dozens of blocks, capturing storm water closer to where it falls.
candidates.explanation: Passage B does not dispute that streams can manage water; it questions whether daylighting is the most effective use of the money, pointing to rain gardens and permeable pavement that capture water across many blocks.

A.rationale: Passage B never denies that streams slow water; its objection is about cost and alternatives.

C.rationale: Passage B says the first question should be about the most effective way to manage water, not about bringing the stream back.

D.rationale: Passage B treats storm-water management as a serious goal; it does not dismiss flooding.

hints: Does Passage B dispute what streams can do, or something else?
What alternatives does Passage B propose?

strategy.explanation: Find Passage B's alternative to daylighting and connect it to the flood claim.

candidates.remember: A critic often concedes the point and questions the priority.

author_checklist.hardness: requires distinguishing a concession from a denial

candidates.stem: Unlike the author of Passage A, the author of Passage B:

choices.A: frames the argument from the perspective of someone responsible for deciding how a city spends its money.
choices.B: acknowledges that daylighting can be expensive.
choices.D: mentions the wildlife that a restored stream can support.

candidates.evidence: As a city planner, though, I have learned to ask what such projects cost and what else the same money might do.
candidates.explanation: Passage B is written in the first person by a city planner who weighs budgets ("what else the same money might do"). Passage A does not adopt that decision-maker's perspective. Both passages acknowledge cost, discuss flooding and mention wildlife, so only A is a true difference.

B.rationale: Passage A also acknowledges cost: "Daylighting is not cheap."

C.rationale: Passage A discusses flooding in detail, so this is not a difference.

hints: For each choice, check whether Passage A does the same thing.
Whose point of view is Passage B written from?

strategy.explanation: Rule out anything both passages do; only one choice is unique to Passage B.

candidates.remember: "Unlike" questions: the answer must be true of one passage only.

author_checklist.hardness: three distractors are true of Passage B but also of Passage A

revision_history.reason: labelled hard; both blind solvers estimated ~83-85% correct (easy). Text unchanged, relabelled easy.

candidates.stem: Mrs. Dalca's statement "I don't know how long. I know what ready looks like" (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that she:

choices.A: is reluctant to share her methods with a new employee.
choices.B: judges the dough by its observable condition rather than by elapsed time.
choices.C: never measures any ingredients when she bakes.
choices.D: privately relies on the wall clock but does not admit it.

candidates.evidence: If it filled in slowly, halfway, she nodded and reached for the scale.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 shows her pressing the dough and watching the dent, a physical sign of readiness. Her remark confirms that she goes by what the dough looks like, not by how many minutes have passed.

A.rationale: She answers the question directly and demonstrates her method; nothing suggests reluctance.

C.rationale: She "reached for the scale," so she does measure; she just doesn't time the rising.

D.rationale: The passage says she "worked without a clock"; nothing supports secret clock-watching.

hints: What does she do just before she reaches for the scale?
Does her method depend on a clock?

strategy.explanation: Pair the quotation with the finger test described in the same paragraph.

candidates.remember: Eliminate choices that the text directly contradicts.
